# From sample to population

<style>
  :root {
    --footer-text:  "Significance testing";
    --qr:           `r qr_css`;
    --lecture:      `r lecture_label`;
  }
</style>

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` when George Shaw of the British Museum examined one of the first platypus specimens, around 1799, he suspected a [hoax]{.hl}, and cut into it to look for stitches.

_Source: Discover Magazine_
:::

## Today

- Samples and populations
- How big is an effect? Cohen's d
- How precise is an estimate? Standard errors and confidence intervals
- Null hypotheses and the `t` statistic
- What a p-value is, and what it is not

## So far

Lectures 3 to 8 described the data we have: means, SDs, slopes, differences between groups.

. . .

But we never care about these 120 vowels. We care about vowels before voiced consonants in general.

. . .

Today: how far can we trust a number computed from a sample?

## Samples and populations

| | Population | Sample |
|:--|:--|:--|
| What it is | everything we want to draw conclusions about: all speakers of a language, all tokens of a vowel | the part of it we actually measured |
| Its mean | a [parameter]{.hl}, written `μ`, usually unknown | a [statistic]{.hl}, written <span style="text-decoration: overline;">x</span>, which we can compute |

. . .

We use the statistic as our estimate of the parameter. Today is about how good that estimate is.

## A population we know

To see how samples behave, simulate a population whose truth we know:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
pop <- rnorm(100000, mean = 140, sd = 25)    # 100,000 vowel durations (ms)
c(mean = mean(pop), sd = sd(pop))
```

## Samples differ

Draw a sample of 10, and compute its mean:

```{r}
set.seed(2)
mean(sample(pop, 10))
mean(sample(pop, 10))
mean(sample(pop, 10))
```

Every sample gives a different estimate.

## Sampling variation

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
set.seed(2)
means <- bind_rows(
  tibble(n = "n = 10", mean = replicate(2000, mean(sample(pop, 10)))),
  tibble(n = "n = 50", mean = replicate(2000, mean(sample(pop, 50))))
)
ggplot(means, aes(x = mean, fill = n)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, colour = floor_col) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 140, colour = mist, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ n) +
  labs(x = "Sample mean (ms)", y = "Count") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

2000 samples each. Dashed: the true mean, 140 ms. Larger samples give less variable estimates.

# Effect size

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` a platypus's bill has about [40,000]{.hl} electroreceptors. Underwater, it closes its eyes, ears and nose, and finds prey by the weak electric signals of their muscles.

_Source: American Museum of Natural History_
:::

## How big is a difference?

Back to lecture 7's vowels:

```{r}
vowels |> summarise(mean = mean(duration), sd = sd(duration), n = n(), .by = voicing)
```

. . .

A difference of about `r round(diff(tapply(vowels$duration, vowels$voicing, mean)))` ms. Big or small?

. . .

That depends on how much durations vary anyway. The same difference is huge if tokens vary by 5 ms, and tiny if they vary by 200 ms.

## Cohen's d

The difference between two means, in units of their standard deviation:

<div class="formula">d = (mean₂ − mean₁) / pooled SD</div>

. . .

The __pooled SD__ combines the two groups' SDs, weighted by their sample sizes:

```{r}
s <- vowels |> summarise(m = mean(duration), sd = sd(duration), n = n(), .by = voicing)

pooled_sd <- sqrt(((s$n[1] - 1) * s$sd[1]^2 + (s$n[2] - 1) * s$sd[2]^2) / (sum(s$n) - 2))
(s$m[2] - s$m[1]) / pooled_sd
```

. . .

The voiced mean is almost 2 SDs above the voiceless mean.

## Cohen's d in R

With the `{effsize}` package (install once with `install.packages("effsize")`):

```{r}
library(effsize)
cohen.d(duration ~ voicing, data = vowels)
```

. . .

`cohen.d()` subtracts the second level from the first, so d is negative here. The size is what matters: `r round(abs(cohen.d(duration ~ voicing, data = vowels)$estimate), 2)`.

## Interpreting d

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.8}
tibble(d = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8, 2)) |>
  mutate(label = paste("d =", d)) |>
  crossing(x = seq(-4, 6, by = 0.02)) |>
  mutate(a = dnorm(x, 0), b = dnorm(x, d)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(a, b), names_to = "group", values_to = "density") |>
  ggplot(aes(x, density, fill = group)) +
  geom_area(position = "identity", alpha = 0.5, colour = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~ label, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none", axis.text = element_blank())
```

Cohen's benchmarks: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. They are rough conventions: what counts as large depends on the field and the measure.

# Standard errors and confidence intervals

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` male platypuses have a venomous [spur]{.hl} on each ankle, most active in the breeding season. The venom is not lethal to humans, but very painful.

_Source: Australian Museum_
:::

## The standard error {.smaller}

How much would a sample mean vary from sample to sample? The __standard error__:

<div class="formula">SE = SD / √n</div>

. . .

Check it against the simulation behind the plot, 2000 sample means for each sample size:

```{r}
set.seed(2)
means <- bind_rows(
  tibble(n = "n = 10", mean = replicate(2000, mean(sample(pop, 10)))),
  tibble(n = "n = 50", mean = replicate(2000, mean(sample(pop, 50))))
)
c(simulated_n10 = sd(means$mean[means$n == "n = 10"]), formula_n10 = 25 / sqrt(10),
  simulated_n50 = sd(means$mean[means$n == "n = 50"]), formula_n50 = 25 / sqrt(50))
```

. . .

The SD describes the [data]{.hl}, and the SE describes the [estimate]{.hl}.

## The SE shrinks with n

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4}
tibble(n = 2:200) |>
  mutate(se = 25 / sqrt(n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, se)) +
  geom_line(colour = hornbill, linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "Sample size (n)", y = "Standard error (ms)")
```

To halve the SE, you need four times as many observations.

## Confidence intervals

A __95% confidence interval__: the estimate, plus and minus about two standard errors.

```{r}
set.seed(3)
x  <- sample(pop, 20)
se <- sd(x) / sqrt(length(x))
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = length(x) - 1)      # about 2.09 for n = 20

c(lower = mean(x) - t_crit * se, mean = mean(x), upper = mean(x) + t_crit * se)
t.test(x)$conf.int
```

## 95% of intervals

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
set.seed(3)
cis <- map_dfr(1:100, \(i) {
  x <- sample(pop, 20)
  ci <- t.test(x)$conf.int
  tibble(i, mean = mean(x), lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2])
}) |>
  mutate(hit = lower < 140 & upper > 140)

ggplot(cis, aes(x = i, y = mean, ymin = lower, ymax = upper, colour = hit)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 140, colour = mist, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(size = 0.25, linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = kingfisher, `FALSE` = orchid)) +
  labs(x = "Sample", y = "Mean and 95% CI (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

100 samples of 20. Pink: the `r sum(!cis$hit)` intervals that miss the true mean. In the long run, 95% of intervals contain it.

## What a confidence interval means

The procedure captures the true value in 95% of samples. Each interval is a range of values that are compatible with the data: narrow intervals come from precise estimates, wide ones from imprecise estimates.

. . .

It does not mean "there is a 95% probability that the true value lies in this particular interval". The true value is fixed, while the interval changes from sample to sample.

# Null hypotheses

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` the platypus is one of the few mammals that [lay eggs]{.hl}, usually two. The young then drink milk from two patches of fur on their mother's belly.

_Source: Australian Museum_
:::

## Null and alternative hypotheses

- The [null hypothesis]{.hl} H₀ says there is no difference: μ_voiced = μ_voiceless
- The alternative hypothesis H₁ says there is one: μ_voiced ≠ μ_voiceless

. . .

Significance testing asks: how compatible are our data with H₀?

. . .

If the data would be very surprising in a world where H₀ is true, we treat that as evidence against H₀.

## A small study

Only 8 vowels per group:

```{r}
set.seed(21)
small <- tibble(
  voicing  = rep(c("voiceless", "voiced"), each = 8),
  duration = round(c(rnorm(8, 120, 20), rnorm(8, 140, 22)))
) |>
  mutate(voicing = fct_relevel(voicing, "voiceless"))

obs_diff <- diff(tapply(small$duration, small$voicing, mean))
obs_diff
```

. . .

Voiced vowels are about `r round(obs_diff)` ms longer. Could a difference this big appear by chance, if voicing had no effect at all?

## Simulating the null

If H₀ is true, the labels "voiced" and "voiceless" are arbitrary. Shuffle them, and see which differences chance alone produces:

```{r}
set.seed(5)
null_diffs <- replicate(5000, {
  shuffled <- sample(small$voicing)
  diff(tapply(small$duration, shuffled, mean))
})
mean(abs(null_diffs) >= abs(obs_diff))
```

. . .

In about `r round(mean(abs(null_diffs) >= abs(obs_diff)) * 100)`% of shuffles, the difference is at least as large as ours.

## Simulating the null

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.2}
tibble(d = null_diffs) |>
  mutate(extreme = abs(d) >= abs(obs_diff)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = d, fill = extreme)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, colour = floor_col, boundary = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1) * obs_diff, colour = mist, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = kingfisher, `TRUE` = orchid)) +
  labs(x = "Difference in means under H₀ (ms)", y = "Count") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

Pink: differences at least as extreme as the observed one (dashed). Our result is not surprising under H₀.

## The t statistic

Instead of simulating, we can measure the difference in units of its standard error:

<div class="formula">t = difference / SE of the difference</div>

```{r}
s_small <- small |> summarise(m = mean(duration), v = var(duration), n = n(), .by = voicing)
se_diff <- sqrt(sum(s_small$v / s_small$n))

obs_diff / se_diff
```

. . .

A t of about `r round(abs(obs_diff / se_diff), 1)`: the difference is only a little larger than its SE.

# p-values

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` platypus fur [glows]{.hl} green or cyan under UV light. The glow was found in museum specimens in 2020; nobody knows yet what it is for.

_Source: Anich et al. (2020), Mammalia_
:::

## The t-distribution {.smaller}

If H₀ is true, t follows a known shape: the __t-distribution__, which depends on the [degrees of freedom]{.hl} (roughly, the sample size).

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.6}
t_obs <- t.test(duration ~ voicing, data = small)
df_obs <- t_obs$parameter
t_val  <- abs(t_obs$statistic)

tibble(t = seq(-5, 5, by = 0.01)) |>
  mutate(density = dt(t, df = df_obs), tail = abs(t) >= t_val) |>
  ggplot(aes(t, density)) +
  geom_area(data = \(d) filter(d, t <= -t_val), fill = orchid, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_area(data = \(d) filter(d, t >= t_val), fill = orchid, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_line(colour = mist, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1) * t_val, colour = mist, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "t", y = "Density")
```

The [p-value]{.hl} is the pink area: the probability of a t at least this extreme, if H₀ were true.

## Computing p {.smaller}

```{r}
t_obs  <- t.test(duration ~ voicing, data = small)
df_obs <- t_obs$parameter          # degrees of freedom
t_val  <- abs(t_obs$statistic)     # observed t, ignoring its sign
2 * pt(-t_val, df = df_obs)        # both tails
```

. . .

Or let `t.test()` do everything:

```{r}
t.test(duration ~ voicing, data = small)
```

## Two tails

- Two-tailed test: H₁ is "a difference in either direction"; both tails count
- One-tailed tests only count one direction. Use them only if the direction was fixed before seeing the data

. . .

`t.test()` is two-tailed by default. Note the `p` matches the shuffling simulation: `r round(2 * pt(-t_val, df = df_obs), 2)` vs `r round(mean(abs(null_diffs) >= abs(obs_diff)), 2)`.

## What a p-value is

The probability of obtaining data at least as extreme as ours, assuming H₀ is true.

. . .

It is not:

- the probability that H₀ is true
- the probability that the result is due to chance
- a measure of how big or important the effect is

. . .

Chapter 10 of Winter is about these misinterpretations: we come back to it in lecture 13.

## Significance

By convention, if `p < α`, with α usually 0.05, the result is called __statistically significant__ and H₀ is rejected.

. . .

- α = 0.05 is a convention, and "significant" means only "surprising under H₀", and says nothing about importance
- p = 0.049 and p = 0.051 are practically the same evidence

## Back to the 120 vowels

```{r}
t.test(duration ~ voicing, data = vowels)
```

. . .

With 60 tokens per group, t is about `r round(abs(t.test(duration ~ voicing, data = vowels)$statistic), 1)`: a difference this large would be extremely unlikely if voicing had no effect.

## Significance is not size {.smaller}

```{r}
set.seed(4)
big <- tibble(group = rep(c("a", "b"), each = 5000),
              y     = c(rnorm(5000, 100, 15), rnorm(5000, 101, 15)))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
tibble(
  study = c("Small study: 8 vowels per group", "Huge study: 5000 per group"),
  `Cohen's d` = c(abs(cohen.d(duration ~ voicing, data = small)$estimate),
                  abs(cohen.d(y ~ group, data = big)$estimate)),
  p = c(t.test(duration ~ voicing, data = small)$p.value, t.test(y ~ group, data = big)$p.value)
) |>
  mutate(`Cohen's d` = round(`Cohen's d`, 2), p = signif(p, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

. . .

A medium effect that is not significant, and a tiny effect that is. The p-value mixes effect size and sample size.

. . .

Always report the [effect size]{.hl} and its [confidence interval]{.hl} alongside p.

## Discussion

Study A tests a pronunciation training with 3,000 learners: ratings improve by 0.1 points on a 7-point scale, p < .001. Study B tests a different training with 12 learners: ratings improve by 1.2 points, p = .09.

- Which result is more convincing? Which training would you try in your own class?
- What would you want to know about each study before deciding?

## t-tests are linear models

```{r}
tidy(lm(duration ~ voicing, data = vowels))
t.test(duration ~ voicing, data = vowels, var.equal = TRUE)$statistic
```

. . .

The slope's `t value` and `p.value` in `lm()` are exactly a t-test (with equal variances assumed). Significance tests for regression coefficients: Chapter 11.

## Reporting

```{r, echo = FALSE}
tt <- t.test(duration ~ voicing, data = vowels)
dd <- abs(cohen.d(duration ~ voicing, data = vowels)$estimate)
diff_ms <- -diff(tt$estimate)
```

With inline R (lecture 3), every number comes from the analysis:

> Vowels before voiced consonants were `r round(-diff_ms, 1)` ms longer than before voiceless consonants (95% CI [`r round(-tt$conf.int[2], 1)`, `r round(-tt$conf.int[1], 1)`]), t(`r round(tt$parameter, 1)`) = `r round(abs(tt$statistic), 2)`, p < .001, d = `r round(dd, 2)`.

. . .

- The effect and its [CI]{.hl}, in the units of the data
- The test statistic, its [degrees of freedom]{.hl}, and p
- A standardised [effect size]{.hl}

# Your turn

## Exercises

With `palmerpenguins::penguins`, keep only Adelie and Chinstrap penguins (use `filter()` and then `droplevels()`):

1. Compare their `body_mass_g`: compute Cohen's d and run a t-test
2. Do the same for `flipper_length_mm`
3. Which difference is significant? Report each with its 95% CI
4. Does the first result show that the two species weigh the same?

## Solutions {.smaller}

```{r}
two <- palmerpenguins::penguins |>
  filter(species %in% c("Adelie", "Chinstrap")) |>
  drop_na(body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm) |>
  mutate(species = droplevels(species))

cohen.d(body_mass_g ~ species, data = two)$estimate
t.test(body_mass_g ~ species, data = two)[c("statistic", "p.value", "conf.int")]
```

## Solutions {.smaller}

```{r}
cohen.d(flipper_length_mm ~ species, data = two)$estimate
t.test(flipper_length_mm ~ species, data = two)[c("statistic", "p.value", "conf.int")]
```

. . .

Flipper length differs clearly; body mass does not reach significance. But a non-significant result is not evidence of no difference: the CI for body mass runs from `r round(t.test(body_mass_g ~ species, data = two)$conf.int[1])` to `r round(t.test(body_mass_g ~ species, data = two)$conf.int[2])` g. The data are compatible with no difference, but just as compatible with differences of that size.

## Summary

::: {.takeaway}
- We estimate population [parameters]{.hl} from sample [statistics]{.hl}
- [Cohen's d]{.hl}: a difference in SD units
- `SE = SD / √n`: how much an estimate varies across samples
- [95% CI]{.hl}: a range of values compatible with the data
- `t` = difference / SE; `p` = how surprising t would be if H₀ were true
- Significant ≠ large ≠ important: report [effect sizes]{.hl} and [CIs]{.hl}
:::
